title: Parikshith
body:
Parikshith

The great war of Kurukshetra had ended, yet its echoes still haunted the land. Within the royal halls of Hastinapura, the last hope of the Pandava lineage awaited birth, for Uttara, the young widow of Abhimanyu, carried in her womb the sole heir who would one day continue the dynasty. But even as life prepared to enter the world, death cast its shadow over it.
Ashwatthama, the son of Dronacharya and the last surviving warrior of the Kaurava side, had pledged to Duryodhana that he would wipe out the Pandavas and their line. In the dead of night he crept into the sleeping camp and slew the sons of the Pandavas born of Draupadi, unarmed and defenseless. When Arjuna discovered the massacre he pursued Ashwatthama across the land, and the two came face to face. Knowing he could not match Arjuna in open battle, Ashwatthama invoked the Brahmashiras-Astra, the most destructive of celestial weapons, and Arjuna answered by invoking his own. The heavens braced for annihilation.
Before the two weapons could collide, Maharishi Vyasa appeared between the warriors and warned them that the impact of such a clash would consume the heavens above, the earth in the middle, and the netherworlds below. He asked them both to withdraw their weapons. Arjuna, honoring dharma, at once drew his back; but Ashwatthama confessed that he possessed the knowledge to launch his weapon and not to recall it — he could only redirect it. Vyasa instructed him to send it toward some place where there were no living beings, where it could cause no harm. In one final act of spite, Ashwatthama turned the weapon instead upon the unborn child in Uttara's womb.
Arjuna pleaded with Krishna to save the child. It is said that the Lord took upon Himself a miniscule form and entered Uttara's womb, where He moved in a protective circle around the infant, absorbing the searing energy of the weapon into Himself. Within the darkness of the womb the child watched the luminous form that circled him, following its motion with wonder, and so, even before his birth, he beheld the Supreme. When he was born, his gaze was unlike that of other infants — steady and searching, as though looking for someone he had already met. For this the sages named him Parikshith, "the one who examines," for all his days he would seek the divine presence he had once seen encircling him.
Parikshith grew into a ruler unmatched in wisdom and strength, a king whose very righteousness held the age of Kali at bay. Kali Yuga had arrived, yet it could find no entry into his kingdom, for justice still sat upon the throne. Taking human form, Kali sought a way in, but each time he was turned aside — he could not corrupt the courts, could not taint the people, and could not touch the mind of the king, whose devotion burned too brightly. At last he resorted to deception, slipping unseen into the golden crown upon Parikshith's head, where he whispered slow poison into the king's thoughts.
One day, after a long hunt, Parikshith was overcome by a thirst like none he had known. Searching for water, he came upon the hermitage of the sage Shamika, who sat in deep meditation and did not stir at the king's approach. Under the influence of Kali within his crown, Parikshith took the silence for an insult; seeing the freshly shed skin of a snake nearby, he lifted it and draped it around the sage's neck. The sage's son, Shringi, learning of the offense, burned with anger and pronounced a curse — that within seven days the serpent Takshaka would strike, and the king would die.
When Parikshith heard of the curse he neither panicked nor sought vengeance. He saw in it not a punishment but an invitation, and resolved that the question was no longer how he would die but how he would spend the days that remained. Handing his throne to his son Janamejaya, he went to the banks of the sacred Ganga. There, as though summoned by destiny, came Shuka Maharishi, the son of Vyasa, a sage untouched by the burdens of the world. Parikshith bowed before him and asked how one might cross beyond death. In answer, over the seven days and nights that followed, Shuka Maharishi narrated to him the Srimad Bhagavatam — not for a king alone, but for all who seek to understand the eternal beyond the fleeting.
